current_component_sources.quote: There’s a significant development in the chiral branch. The team has assembled and internally checked a different ungauged construction in which the unwanted boundary is gapped, the original free bulk is retained beyond a fixed boundary region, and the desired particles appear on the opposite side. The extra local resources are finite, though their size has not been evaluated and could be enormous. This is stronger than the earlier construction because it uses a different chiral particle set and appears to remove an important boundary obstacle. It is still a theoretical result with internal checks, not an external verification. The decisive next test is coupling it to a genuine quantum gauge field and showing the full low-energy theory has no unwanted sector. I’m continuing that attack; I wouldn’t call the civilisation-level goal achieved.
current_component_sources.range_scope: Complete additional visible internally checked ungauged boundary claim: different chiral particle set, fixed boundary region and finite unquantified local resources. Quantum gauge coupling and exclusion of unwanted full low-energy sectors remain open. No proof package supplied.

current_component_sources.quote: Yes. The most substantial work is still the chiral-physics construction: an internally checked way to gap the unwanted mirror boundary while retaining a desired Weyl-particle signal on the opposite face. If completed, this could help construct a class of chiral quantum theories on a lattice. It is not yet a completed theory or a civilisation-level breakthrough. The latest decisive tests exposed the remaining gap: we cannot yet rule out additional low-energy states in the full finite slab, and the construction’s global symmetry does not establish a dynamically gauged theory. Two attempted shortcuts failed; they do not disprove the construction. I’m putting the main effort into the actual completeness obstacle rather than treating the boundary result as the goal. The independent searches also tested new computation and molecular/biological ideas. The computation candidates did not beat the established alternatives convincingly, so I’m not counting them as breakthroughs. The molecular work is still searching for a concrete mechanism that earns its claimed capability. One operational detail: the previous active agents were no longer running after the session recovered. Their saved work remains, but I can’t honestly say they kept working through that interruption. I’ve restarted six agent assignments: two checking the latest results, two attacking the chiral obstacle, and two pursuing independent capability ideas. I’ll continue integrating and testing their work myself.
current_component_sources.range_scope: Complete 04:20 visible limit/status update: boundary gap and opposite-face signal do not establish finite-slab completeness or dynamical gauging;extra states remain unexcluded,two shortcuts failed without disproving construction,reported agent interruption/restarts and no established independent breakthrough.

current_component_sources.quote: A meaningful development since my update: we now have a candidate proof that the unwanted extra low-energy states can be excluded for a finite-width device of any fixed cross-sectional size, provided the device is made sufficiently long. An independent internal audit has checked the main construction, including a subtle mismatch between the mathematical descriptions of the two systems. The qualification matters: the required length and computational resources may grow badly with the cross-section. This does not yet establish the fixed-resource large-system result or dynamical gauging, and it has not had external review. I’m checking those remaining steps rather than treating this as the finished breakthrough.
current_component_sources.range_scope: Full visible source update: candidate finite-width exclusion and later proposed costly polynomial slab-thickness/area bound;source internal checks reported,ungauged scope and confidence retained.

current_component_sources.quote: The finite-device result has become more concrete: we have a proposed polynomial bound on how the slab thickness must grow with its cross-sectional area to exclude extra low-energy states. Two internal checks have examined the construction and its resource accounting. It also appears to give the complete free Weyl-particle spectrum, including multiplicities, along a growing-device sequence. This is stronger than the earlier particle-signal result, but the bound is extremely costly and the proof still needs external scrutiny. Most importantly, it is still an ungauged matter construction. We have not shown that it produces a chiral gauge theory, and that is where the next decisive work is focused.
current_component_sources.range_scope: Full visible source update: candidate finite-width exclusion and later proposed costly polynomial slab-thickness/area bound;source internal checks reported,ungauged scope and confidence retained.

current_component_sources.quote: The gauge investigation has exposed a real obstacle: the longer slab that gives us the complete matter spectrum also makes the bulk respond more strongly to a shared gauge field. We can’t assume the desired interaction stays fixed as the device grows. We tested one possible fix, confining the gauge field near the surface. In a controlled limit it creates a new unwanted mirror boundary, so it doesn’t solve the problem. I’m working on whether that new boundary can itself be gapped while retaining the gauge field and the desired particles. No interacting chiral gauge theory has been established yet.
current_component_sources.range_scope: Complete visible gauge obstacle: growing-slab shared-field bulk response;surface localization produces new mirror boundary in controlled limit;new boundary gapping open,no interacting chiral gauge theory.

current_component_sources.quote: A further update: the gauge work has produced a possible way to certify that unwanted charge-constraint violations stay out of low-energy states, including for a class of finite quantum-link models. It has passed internal checks, but it still doesn’t solve the missing mirror separation or establish an interacting chiral gauge theory. I also tested a different route: a proposed algorithm to certify all low-energy states of certain quantum impurity systems. The mathematics has passed an internal audit, but a concrete benchmark exposed a huge cost: its guarantee required a problem vastly larger than established numerical methods use. So I’m treating it as a possible rigorous certificate, not the breakthrough or a practical speedup. Neither result has been externally verified.
